claim: Mitochondrial import deficiency causes cellular toxicity due to the accumulation of non-imported mitochondrial precursor proteins, termed mitoprotein-induced stress.
source: Mitochondrial import deficiency causes cellular toxicity due to the accumulation of non-imported mitochondrial precursor proteins, termed mitoprotein-induced stress.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by citations to prior work in the field (Wang and Chen, 2015; Wrobel et al., 2015) as shown in the introduction.

claim: Ilv2 is a mitochondrial matrix enzyme in isoleucine and valine biosynthesis.
source: Ilv2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a mitochondrial matrix enzyme in isoleucine and valine biosynthesis (Falco et al., 1985)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Falco et al., 1985.

claim: Ilv2-GFP localized to the nucleus in over 80% of aged yeast cells.
source: Ilv2-GFP also localized to the nucleus in over 80% of aged cells, as indicated by diffuse GFP fluorescence within a region surrounded by the nuclear pore protein Nup49-mCherry (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and quantification of cells.

claim: The mitochondrial network undergoes extensive fragmentation and depolarization during replicative aging in budding yeast.
source: We previously showed that the mitochondrial network undergoes extensive fragmentation and depolarization during replicative aging in budding yeast, which is defined as the number of times an individual yeast cell undergoes division (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012).

claim: Tom70 does not rely on mitochondrial membrane potential for its mitochondrial localization.
source: In contrast to Tom70, which does not rely on mitochondrial membrane potential for its mitochondrial localization (Söllner et al., 1990)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Söllner et al., 1990.

claim: Treatment of cells with FCCP caused Ilv2-GFP accumulation in the nucleus.
source: Consistent with that idea, treatment of cells with the mitochondrial IM depolarizing agent trifluoromethoxy carbonyl cyanide phenylhydrazone (FCCP) (Parker, 1965) also caused Ilv2-GFP accumulation in the nucleus, which was marked with 4′,6-Diamidine-2′-phenylindole dihydrochloride (DAPI) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Nuclear localization of Ilv2 did not result from GFP-tagging.
source: Nuclear localization did not result from GFP-tagging, as indirect immunofluorescence showed a similar nuclear localization for native Ilv2 (Figure 1C) as well as functional C-terminally FLAG-tagged Ilv2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) in FCCP-treated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, and functional data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ilv2-GFP localized to the nucleus in cells conditionally depleted of Tom40.
source: Furthermore, Ilv2-GFP localized to the nucleus in cells conditionally depleted of the essential OM protein import channel Tom40 (Mnaimneh et al., 2004; Vestweber et al., 1989; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D and citations to prior work on Tom40.

claim: Nuclear localization of Ilv2 was not caused by off-target effects of FCCP, but was specific to defects in mitochondrial protein import.
source: indicating that nuclear localization was not caused by off-target effects of FCCP, but was specific to defects in mitochondrial protein import.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Tom40 depletion (a genetic method) produces the same phenotype as FCCP treatment (a pharmacological method).

claim: Higher-molecular-weight forms of Ilv2, Ilv2-GFP, and Ilv2-HA accumulated in cells treated with FCCP.
source: Consistent with that idea, western blot analysis revealed that higher-molecular-weight forms of Ilv2, Ilv2-GFP, and Ilv2-HA accumulated in cells treated with FCCP (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D, 1E, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mitochondrial proteins are synthesized with an N-terminal MTS extension that is proteolytically removed from the mature peptide only after they transit the mitochondrial IM.
source: Mitochondrial proteins such as Ilv2 are synthesized with an N-terminal MTS extension that is proteolytically removed from the mature peptide only after they transit the mitochondrial IM (Mossmann et al., 2012; Pfanner et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mossmann et al., 2012; Pfanner et al., 2019).

claim: The higher-molecular-weight form of Ilv2 in FCCP-treated cells likely represents the immature, precursor form of the protein.
source: Thus, the higher-molecular-weight form of Ilv2 in FCCP-treated cells likely represents the immature, precursor form of the protein.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the knowledge that MTSs are removed after import and the observation of higher molecular weight forms in FCCP-treated cells.

claim: The precursor form of Ilv2-HA was specifically enriched in nuclear fractions isolated from FCCP-treated cells.
source: In support of the idea that the non-imported pool of Ilv2 localizes to the nucleus, the precursor form of Ilv2-HA was specifically enriched in nuclear fractions isolated from FCCP-treated cells, while other mitochondrial proteins, including Tom70, Tim44, as well as the mature form of Ilv2-HA, were excluded (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear fractionation data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Only newly synthesized Ilv2 localized to the nucleus upon FCCP treatment, while Ilv2 already present in mitochondria did not.
source: We found that only newly synthesized Ilv2 (Ilv2 New, RFP tagged) localized to the nucleus upon FCCP treatment, while Ilv2 already present in mitochondria (Ilv2 Old, GFP tagged) did not (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by RITE tag-switching data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: When the translocation of Ilv2 into mitochondria is blocked by genetic or pharmacologic impairment of mitochondrial import, the non-imported precursor form of Ilv2 alternatively localizes to the nucleus.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that when the translocation of Ilv2 into mitochondria is blocked by genetic or pharmacologic impairment of mitochondrial import, the non-imported precursor form of Ilv2 alternatively localizes to the nucleus.
evidence: This claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations presented in the preceding text and figures.

claim: 6.4% of the mitochondrial proteins analyzed exhibited nuclear localization in FCCP-treated cells (class 1).
source: We found that 6.4% of the mitochondrial proteins analyzed behaved like Ilv2, exhibiting nuclear localization in FCCP-treated cells (class 1, Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 8.2% of mitochondrial proteins continued localization to the mitochondrion after membrane depolarization (class 2).
source: These included continued localization to the mitochondrion (class 2, e.g., Tom20, 8.2% of all proteins)
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 36.1% of mitochondrial proteins accumulated in the cytoplasm after membrane depolarization (class 3).
source: accumulation in the cytoplasm (class 3, e.g., Acp1, 36.1% of all proteins)
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 2.7% of mitochondrial proteins localized to the ER after membrane depolarization (class 4).
source: localization to the ER (class 4, e.g., Mir1, 2.7% of all proteins)
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 42.2% of mitochondrial proteins exhibited reduced overall abundance to the point of being nearly undetectable after membrane depolarization (class 5).
source: and reduced overall abundance to the point of being nearly undetectable (class 5, e.g., Cox15, 42.2% of all proteins).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Most class 2 proteins that continued to localize to depolarized mitochondria were mitochondrial OM proteins that do not require a membrane potential for mitochondrial targeting.
source: Most class 2 proteins that continued to localize to depolarized mitochondria were mitochondrial OM proteins that do not require a membrane potential for mitochondrial targeting (Wiedemann and Pfanner, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data and a citation to prior work (Wiedemann and Pfanner, 2017).

claim: Class 3 (cytoplasm) proteins were largely soluble proteins, several of which were previously found to be enriched in cytosolic extracts isolated from mitochondrial import-deficient yeast.
source: Class 3 (cytoplasm) proteins were largely soluble proteins, several of which (e.g., Idh1, Idh2, Mss116, and Cis1) were previously found to be enriched in cytosolic extracts isolated from mitochondrial import-deficient yeast (Wang and Chen, 2015; Weidberg and Amon, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data and citations to prior work (Wang and Chen, 2015; Weidberg and Amon, 2018).

claim: ER-localized class 4 proteins were generally integral IM and OM proteins, some of which were previously reported to localize to the ER in cells with compromised mitochondrial import.
source: ER-localized class 4 proteins were generally integral IM and OM proteins, some of which were previously reported to localize to the ER in cells with compromised mitochondrial import (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data and a citation to prior work (Hansen et al., 2018).

claim: The decline in class 5 protein abundance was either completely or partially blunted by proteasome inhibition via MG-132 depending on the individual protein substrate.
source: Interestingly, further analysis indicated that the decline in class 5 protein abundance was either completely or partially blunted by proteasome inhibition via MG-132 depending on the individual protein substrate (Figure 2C,D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E), implicating the proteasome in their destruction.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2C, 2D, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Nuclear-localized class 1 proteins were predominantly mitochondrial matrix enzymes, including numerous members of the TCA cycle.
source: Nuclear-localized class 1 proteins were predominantly mitochondrial matrix enzymes, including numerous members of the TCA cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The decline in steady-state levels of Ilv2-GFP and Ilv2-HA upon FCCP treatment was blunted in the presence of proteasome inhibitor MG-132.
source: In support of that idea, the decline in steady-state levels of Ilv2-GFP and Ilv2-HA upon FCCP treatment was blunted in the presence of proteasome inhibitor MG-132 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ilv2 decline was prevented in strains lacking a combination of three E3 ubiquitin ligases San1, Ubr1, and Doa10 (E3 KO).
source: Ilv2 decline was also prevented in strains lacking a combination of three E3 ubiquitin ligases that operate in nuclear-associated protein quality control, San1 (Gardner et al., 2005; Samant et al., 2018), Ubr1 (Prasad et al., 2010), and Doa10 (Deng and Hochstrasser, 2006; Swanson et al., 2001) (E3 KO) (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C, and citations to prior work on these E3 ligases.

claim: No combination of single or double knockouts of San1, Ubr1, or Doa10 completely prevented loss of Ilv2 upon mitochondrial depolarization, suggesting these ligases act redundantly.
source: No combination of single or double knockouts completely prevented loss of Ilv2 upon mitochondrial depolarization, suggesting these ligases act redundantly to promote non-imported mitochondrial protein clearance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The addition of proteasome inhibitor or deletion of San1, Ubr1, and Doa10 each led to a marked elevation in the higher-molecular-weight precursor form of Ilv2 in the presence of FCCP.
source: Importantly, the addition of proteasome inhibitor or deletion of the aforementioned E3 ligases each led to a marked elevation in the higher-molecular-weight precursor form of Ilv2 in the presence of FCCP, suggesting the immature, Ilv2 precursor was the form of the protein specifically marked for proteasome clearance (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A, 3B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The half-life of the Ilv2, Ilv2-HA, and Ilv2-GFP precursor forms were altered in the E3 KO strain, while the mature forms were unaffected.
source: In line with this observation, cycloheximide-chase analysis demonstrated that the half-life of the Ilv2, Ilv2-HA, and Ilv2-GFP precursor forms were altered in the E3 KO strain, while the mature forms were unaffected (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by cycloheximide-chase data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Ilv2 was ubiquitylated in the presence of FCCP in a San1-, Ubr1-, and Doa10-dependent manner.
source: Furthermore, ubiquitin immunoprecipitation assays indicated that Ilv2 was ubiquitylated in the presence of FCCP in a San1-, Ubr1-, and Doa10-dependent manner (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ubiquitin immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Proteasome-dependent degradation of a non-nuclear class 5 substrate (Lat1) was unaffected in the E3 KO strain, indicating that additional E3 ligases promote clearance of non-nuclear localized mitochondrial precursors.
source: Proteasome-dependent degradation of a non-nuclear class 5 substrate (Lat1) was unaffected in the E3 KO strain, indicating that additional E3 ligases promote clearance of non-nuclear localized mitochondrial precursors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: GFP-tagged versions of Dld1 and Dld2 were eliminated in a proteasome and San1/Ubr1/Doa10-dependent manner.
source: Moreover, we found that our observations extend beyond Ilv2, as GFP-tagged versions of two other nuclear candidates identified in our screen, Dld1 and Dld2, (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C) were also eliminated in a proteasome and San1/Ubr1/Doa10-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-F.

claim: A subset of non-imported mitochondrial proteins are subjected to nuclear-associated protein quality control when their import into mitochondria is impaired.
source: Thus, a subset of non-imported mitochondrial proteins are subjected to nuclear-associated protein quality control when their import into mitochondria is impaired.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: Ilv2-GFP accumulated in nuclear-associated foci that resembled previously described juxtanuclear or intranuclear protein aggregate compartments.
source: In line with that hypothesis, we noticed that in addition to diffuse nuclear localization, a portion of Ilv2-GFP accumulated in nuclear-associated foci that resembled previously described juxtanuclear (Kaganovich et al., 2008) or intranuclear (Miller et al., 2015) protein aggregate compartments (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and citations to prior work (Kaganovich et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2015).

claim: Ilv2-GFP foci were adjacent to the DAPI-stained nucleus, excluded the mitochondrial marker Tom70-mCherry, and were present in a high percentage of FCCP-treated cells.
source: These foci were adjacent to the DAPI-stained nucleus, excluded the mitochondrial marker Tom70-mCherry, and were present in a high percentage of FCCP-treated cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4B and quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: The intensity of Ilv2-GFP foci increased in the E3 KO strain.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the intensity of Ilv2-GFP foci increased in the E3 KO strain (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Dld1 and Dld2 localized to nuclear-associated foci, but only in strains lacking the E3 ligase degradation machinery.
source: Moreover, Dld1 and Dld2, which are degraded more robustly than Ilv2, also localized to nuclear-associated foci, but only in strains lacking the E3 ligase degradation machinery (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: A twofold increase in expression of Ilv2-GFP from a single-copy plasmid resulted in constitutive localization of Ilv2-GFP to the nucleus and nuclear associated protein foci.
source: However, we did find that a twofold increase in expression of Ilv2-GFP from a single-copy plasmid resulted in constitutive localization of Ilv2-GFP to the nucleus and nuclear associated protein foci (see Figure 5B–D)
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Overexpression of Ilv2-GFP resulted in severe growth defects in both wild-type and E3 KO strains.
source: and resulted in severe growth defects in both wild-type and E3 KO strains (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: NES addition to Ilv2-GFP resulted in exclusion of Ilv2-GFP from the nucleus and lack of Ilv2-GFP turnover in the presence of FCCP.
source: NES addition resulted in exclusion of Ilv2-GFP from the nucleus and lack of Ilv2-GFP turnover in the presence of FCCP (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy and western blot data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Expression of nuclear-excluded Ilv2 in cells led to severe growth defects.
source: Interestingly, expression of nuclear-excluded Ilv2 in cells led to severe growth defects (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Non-imported Ilv2 is toxic to cells and nuclear-based proteasome destruction and aggregate sequestration may act in coordination to mitigate this toxicity.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that non-imported Ilv2 is toxic to cells and that nuclear-based proteasome destruction and aggregate sequestration may act in coordination to mitigate this toxicity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: Plasmid-derived FL-Ilv2-GFP localized to the nucleus and nuclear-associated foci, and its abundance declined with FCCP.
source: Like endogenous Ilv2-GFP (Endo), plasmid-derived FL-Ilv2-GFP localized to the nucleus and nuclear-associated foci, and its abundance declined with FCCP (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy and western blot data shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: Ilv2 lacking an MTS (ΔMTS-Ilv2-GFP) constitutively localized to the nucleus even in the absence of FCCP, but never formed nuclear-associated foci or decreased in abundance with FCCP.
source: By contrast, Ilv2 lacking an MTS (ΔMTS-Ilv2-GFP) constitutively localized to the nucleus even in the absence of FCCP, but never formed nuclear-associated foci or decreased in abundance with FCCP (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy and western blot data shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: MTSIlv2-GFP localized to mitochondria and exhibited no nuclear localization, puncta formation, or changes in total abundance with FCCP.
source: MTSIlv2-GFP localized to mitochondria and exhibited no nuclear localization, puncta formation, or changes in total abundance with FCCP (Figure 5B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy and western blot data shown in Figure 5B-E.

claim: Information in the mature, C-terminal portion of Ilv2 is necessary and sufficient for nuclear localization, but the presence of an MTS is required for non-imported Ilv2 degradation and sequestration into nuclear-associated foci.
source: Thus, information in the mature, C-terminal portion of Ilv2 is necessary and sufficient for nuclear localization, but the presence of an MTS is required for non-imported Ilv2 degradation and sequestration into nuclear-associated foci.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: Overexpressed Ilv2 lacking its MTS did not slow cell growth, and neither did overexpressed MTSIlv2-GFP alone.
source: In contrast to overexpressed FL Ilv2-GFP, which impaired growth of both wild type and E3 KO cells in the presence or absence of FCCP (Figure 4E), overexpressed Ilv2 lacking its MTS did not slow cell growth, and neither did overexpressed MTSIlv2-GFP alone (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The presence of an MTS on unimported Ilv2 rendered the protein toxic and promoted its subsequent quality control.
source: Thus, the presence of an MTS on unimported Ilv2 rendered the protein toxic and promoted its subsequent quality control.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: Dld2 lacking its MTS constitutively localized to the nucleus, but was not subjected to degradation or sequestered into nuclear foci, and was no longer toxic to cells.
source: Like Ilv2, Dld2 lacking its MTS constitutively localized to the nucleus, but was not subjected to degradation or sequestered into nuclear foci, and was no longer toxic to cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-F.

claim: Degradation and toxicity of Cox15 and Lat1, which are degraded by a non-nuclear proteasome pathway, also required an N-terminal MTS.
source: Moreover, degradation and toxicity of Cox15 and Lat1, which are degraded by a non-nuclear proteasome pathway, also required an N-terminal MTS (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and growth assay data shown in Figure 5G,H.

claim: The presence of an MTS on an unimported mitochondrial protein drives toxicity and targets the protein for quality control.
source: Thus, the presence of an MTS on an unimported mitochondrial protein drives toxicity and targets the protein for quality control.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-tagged full-length Ilv2 (FL), but not MTS-deleted Ilv2-GFP (ΔMTS) or MTSIlv2 only (MTS)-GFP, decreased import of Su9-DHFR into isolated mitochondria.
source: We found that overexpression of GFP-tagged full-length Ilv2 (FL), but not MTS-deleted Ilv2-GFP (ΔMTS) or MTSIlv2 only (MTS)-GFP, decreased import of Su9-DHFR into isolated mitochondria, as indicated by reduced formation of the mature form of Su9-DHFR during incubation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro import assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Mitochondria isolated from strains overexpressing FL-Ilv2-GFP contained lower steady-state levels of mitochondrial IM protein Tim54, but not the OM proteins Tom70 and Tom20.
source: Consistent with these effects, we also found that mitochondria isolated from strains overexpressing FL-Ilv2-GFP contained lower steady-state levels of mitochondrial IM protein Tim54, but not the OM proteins Tom70 and Tom20 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The reduction in the import of Su9-DHFR and steady-state abundance of mitochondrial proteins in strains overexpressing Ilv2-GFP was not as strong as those observed in mitochondria isolated from cells treated with FCCP.
source: The reduction in the import of Su9-DHFR and steady-state abundance of mitochondrial proteins in strains overexpressing Ilv2-GFP was not as strong as those observed in mitochondria isolated from cells treated with FCCP (Figure 6C,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro import assay and western blot data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Ilv2 overexpression led to the cytoplasmic accumulation of the mitochondrial precursor Idh1-GFP in over 30% of cells, as compared to nearly 100% cytoplasmic accumulation observed in cells treated with FCCP.
source: Consistent with this observation, Ilv2 overexpression led to the cytoplasmic accumulation of the mitochondrial precursor Idh1-GFP in over 30% of cells, as compared to nearly 100% cytoplasmic accumulation observed in cells treated with FCCP (Figure 6E,F, and as reported in screen results reported in Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Overexpressed full-length Ilv2-GFP partially blocks mitochondrial import, but not to the same extent as the mitochondrial depolarizing agent FCCP.
source: Together, these results indicate that overexpressed full-length Ilv2-GFP partially blocks mitochondrial import, but not to the same extent as the mitochondrial depolarizing agent FCCP.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the preceding section.

claim: Ilv2-NES-GFP had little to no impact on the in vitro import of Su9-DHFR and had only mild effects on the steady-state levels of Tim54 and Aco1 in isolated mitochondria.
source: Remarkably, we found that Ilv2-NES-GFP, despite its high toxicity, had little to no impact on the in vitro import of Su9-DHFR and had only mild effects on the steady-state levels of Tim54 and Aco1 in isolated mitochondria (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro import assay and western blot data shown in Figure 6G,H.

claim: The toxicity of non-imported Ilv2 cannot be completely attributed to its ability to act as a mitochondrial import clogger, and likely stems from additional deleterious effects of the protein on unidentified cellular processes.
source: Given the fact that this version of Ilv2 is highly toxic to cells both in the presence and in the absence of FCCP, it seems that the toxicity of non-imported Ilv2 cannot be completely attributed to its ability to act as a mitochondrial import clogger, and likely stems from additional deleterious effects of the protein on unidentified cellular processes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that Ilv2-NES-GFP is toxic but does not significantly block import.

claim: The nucleus is an important quality control destination for sequestering and destroying non-imported mitochondrial proteins.
source: Here, we surveyed the mitochondrial proteome under conditions of mitochondrial import impairment to get a clearer picture of the full spectrum of fates for non-imported mitochondrial proteins. We found that mitochondrial precursors accumulate in many regions of the cell and identified the nucleus as an important quality control destination for sequestering and destroying non-imported mitochondrial proteins.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The N-terminal MTS is a major driver of non-imported protein toxicity.
source: Moreover, we demonstrated that the N-terminal MTS is a major driver of non-imported protein toxicity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Non-imported mitochondrial proteins represent a large class of potential substrates for nuclear protein quality control.
source: Our findings also indicate that non-imported mitochondrial proteins represent a large class of potential substrates for nuclear protein quality control.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the screen data showing multiple mitochondrial proteins localize to the nucleus upon import failure.

claim: Non-imported mitochondrial proteins may synergize with other aggregate-prone proteins to overwhelm protein quality control systems during aging and disease.
source: This discovery raises the intriguing possibility that non-imported mitochondrial proteins may synergize with other aggregate-prone proteins to overwhelm protein quality control systems during aging and disease (Park et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential implications of the findings, supported by a citation to prior work (Park et al., 2013).

claim: Recognition and destruction of mitochondrial precursors by the mitoNUC pathway requires the presence of an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence.
source: Recognition and destruction of mitochondrial precursors by the mitoNUC pathway requires the presence of an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence and is mediated by combined action of the E3 ubiquitin ligases San1, Ubr1, and Doa10.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Destruction of mitochondrial precursors by the mitoNUC pathway is mediated by combined action of the E3 ubiquitin ligases San1, Ubr1, and Doa10.
source: Recognition and destruction of mitochondrial precursors by the mitoNUC pathway requires the presence of an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence and is mediated by combined action of the E3 ubiquitin ligases San1, Ubr1, and Doa10.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Impaired breakdown of precursors leads to alternative sequestration in nuclear-associated foci.
source: Impaired breakdown of precursors leads to alternative sequestration in nuclear-associated foci.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The nucleus is an important destination for the disposal of non-imported mitochondrial precursors.
source: These results identify the nucleus as an important destination for the disposal of non-imported mitochondrial precursors.
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A number of non-imported mitochondrial proteins localize to the nucleus during mitochondrial impairment in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Here, we cataloged the location and steady-state abundance of mitochondrial precursor proteins during mitochondrial impairment in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. We found that a number of non-imported mitochondrial proteins localize to the nucleus, where they are subjected to proteasome-dependent degradation through a process we term nuclear-associated mitoprotein degradation (mitoNUC).
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by the screen data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Non-imported mitochondrial proteins that localize to the nucleus are subjected to proteasome-dependent degradation through a process termed nuclear-associated mitoprotein degradation (mitoNUC).
source: We found that a number of non-imported mitochondrial proteins localize to the nucleus, where they are subjected to proteasome-dependent degradation through a process we term nuclear-associated mitoprotein degradation (mitoNUC).
evidence: This is a summary statement from the abstract supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of aging and associated with many age-related and metabolic diseases.
source: Mitochondrial dysfunction is a hallmark of aging and associated with many age-related and metabolic diseases (Wallace, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Wallace, 2005).

claim: Mitochondrial impairment prevents the import of thousands of mitochondrial resident proteins that rely on an efficient mitochondrial membrane potential for translocation into the organelle.
source: Mitochondrial impairment disrupts metabolic pathways housed within the mitochondrion and also prevents the import of thousands of mitochondrial resident proteins that rely on an efficient mitochondrial membrane potential for translocation into the organelle (Martin et al., 1991; Pagliarini et al., 2008; Wiedemann and Pfanner, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Martin et al., 1991; Pagliarini et al., 2008; Wiedemann and Pfanner, 2017).

claim: Non-imported mitochondrial precursor proteins are toxic for cells.
source: Recent studies have shown that non-imported mitochondrial precursor proteins are toxic for cells and identified several cellular pathways that combat this stress (Boos et al., 2019; Boos et al., 2020; Hansen et al., 2018; Itakura et al., 2016; Mårtensson et al., 2019; Wang and Chen, 2015; Weidberg and Amon, 2018; Wrobel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Cells protect against mitoprotein-induced stress through downregulation of cellular translation.
source: These systems, which are collectively referred to as the mitoprotein-induced stress response (Boos et al., 2020), protect cells during times of mitochondrial import deficiency through a variety of mechanisms, including downregulation of cellular translation (Wang and Chen, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Wang and Chen, 2015; Boos et al., 2020).

claim: Cells protect against mitoprotein-induced stress through upregulation of proteasome and chaperone capacity through a process termed UPRam.
source: upregulation of proteasome and chaperone capacity through a process termed UPRam (unfolded protein response activated by mistargeting of proteins) (Boos et al., 2019; Wrobel et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Boos et al., 2019; Wrobel et al., 2015).

claim: Non-imported mitochondrial precursors are destroyed at the mitochondrial surface through mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD).
source: destruction of non-imported mitochondrial precursors at the mitochondrial surface through mitochondrial-associated degradation (MAD) (Metzger et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Metzger et al., 2020).

claim: Non-imported mitochondrial precursors are destroyed through mitochondrial translocation-associated degradation (mitoTAD).
source: mitochondrial translocation-associated degradation (mitoTAD) (Mårtensson et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Mårtensson et al., 2019).

claim: Non-imported mitochondrial precursors are destroyed through mitochondrial-compromised import response (mitoCPR).
source: mitochondrial-compromised import response (mitoCPR) (Weidberg and Amon, 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Weidberg and Amon, 2018).

claim: Non-imported mitochondrial precursors are destroyed through mitochondrial-associated ribosome quality control (mitoRQC).
source: and mitochondrial-associated ribosome quality control (mitoRQC) (Izawa et al., 2017; Su et al., 2019; Zurita Rendón et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Izawa et al., 2017; Su et al., 2019; Zurita Rendón et al., 2018).

claim: Ubiquilin-dependent triaging of mitochondrial membrane proteins for degradation is a mechanism to combat mitoprotein-induced stress.
source: ubiquilin-dependent triaging of mitochondrial membrane proteins for degradation (Itakura et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Itakura et al., 2016).

claim: Endoplasmic sequestration followed by destruction via the conserved protein Ema19 is a mechanism to combat mitoprotein-induced stress.
source: and endoplasmic sequestration followed by either destruction via the conserved protein Ema19 (Laborenz et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Laborenz et al., 2021).

claim: Re-delivery of non-imported mitochondrial precursors via an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) surface retrieval pathway (ER-SURF) is a mechanism to combat mitoprotein-induced stress.
source: or re-delivery of non-imported mitochondrial precursors via an endoplasmic reticulum (ER) surface retrieval pathway (ER-SURF) (Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Hansen et al., 2018).

claim: The N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS) is necessary for non-imported precursor protein induced-toxicity, degradation, and sequestration into nuclear-associated foci, but dispensable for nuclear localization.
source: Interestingly, we determined that the N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS) (Omura, 1998) is necessary for non-imported precursor protein induced-toxicity, degradation, and sequestration into nuclear-associated foci, but dispensable for nuclear localization.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The presence of an MTS is required for degradation and toxicity of non-imported proteins that localize to cellular regions other than the nucleus.
source: The presence of an MTS is also required for degradation and toxicity of non-imported proteins that localize to cellular regions other than the nucleus, implicating the MTS as a major driver of non-imported precursor toxicity.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nuclear accumulation of non-imported precursors arises during cellular aging.
source: Finally, we show that nuclear accumulation of non-imported precursors arises during cellular aging.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The failure to remove and clear MTSs leads to toxicity.
source: The MTS is removed by mitochondrial-localized proteases after import (Mossmann et al., 2012), and failure to remove and clear MTSs leads to toxicity (Mossmann et al., 2014; Poveda-Huertes et al., 2020; Roise et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mossmann et al., 2014; Poveda-Huertes et al., 2020; Roise et al., 1986).

claim: The failure to degrade some non-imported mitochondrial proteins leads to toxicity because the undegraded precursors clog mitochondrial import pores.
source: Recent studies have shown that the failure to degrade some non-imported mitochondrial proteins leads to toxicity because the undegraded precursors clog mitochondrial import pores (Mårtensson et al., 2019; Weidberg and Amon, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Mårtensson et al., 2019; Weidberg and Amon, 2018).

claim: Misfolded proteins can be sequestered into nuclear-associated aggregates when their proteasomal clearance is impaired.
source: Prior studies showed that misfolded proteins can be sequestered into nuclear-associated aggregates when their proteasomal clearance is impaired (Kaganovich et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work (Kaganovich et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2015).

claim: The eukaryotic nucleus harbors a large proportion of cellular proteasomes and is a quality control destination for misfolded proteins.
source: The eukaryotic nucleus harbors a large proportion of cellular proteasomes and is a quality control destination for misfolded proteins (Enam et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work (Enam et al., 2018).
